utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please take your seats. Will you have the accused brought in, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] First of all, I'd like to say good afternoon to the interpreters and the Prosecution and the Defence, and to hear the news from Mr. Greaves and your computer, whether it is functioning properly. Is everything in order?

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: I'm afraid I spent part of the early afternoon trying to destroy some of the equipment of the Tribunal. It's my fault entirely; a momentary lapse of concentration. I'm sorry I caused you any delay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would just like to tell you that when you find a mistake in the transcript, to check your equipment as well, please. Thank you. Mr. Nice?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The next witness is Mustafa Ramic. I trust you have his summaries. He seeks no order of protection. May he be brought in, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Ramic, can you hear me? You can hear me. Very well. You are now going to remind us of your name and surname and your date and place of birth. There are no protection measures. You can tell us your name, your surname, your place and date of birth, please, to begin with.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My name is Mustafa Ramic. I was born on the 6th of February, 1942, in Brcko. At present I reside in Sarajevo. By profession I am a machine engineer, graduated from university, and I am employed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That will be enough for the time being. Would you take the oath, please, according to the formula that the usher will hand you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Ramic. You can sit down now. You have accepted to come to the Tribunal and appear in this present hearing in front of the International Tribunal, and it is the Prosecutor against Mr. Goran Jelisic, who is to your left, between the two U.N. guards. We wanted to tell you that you were, first of all, going to hear questions put to you by the Prosecution, and we'll then have questions from the Defence. Then, of course, the Judges will decide whether or not to ask you any additional questions. I should like to tell you that you can feel very calm. You will sitting in front of Judges. It is always difficult, I know. If you need any break or a pause in the proceedings, please ask for it, and you will see that everything will evolve in the best possible terms. Mr. Nice is the representative of the Prosecution, and I give the floor to the Prosecutor. Examined by Mr. Nice:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Ramic, were you born and did you live most of your life before the war in Brcko? Indeed, was your brother to become the president of the Brcko SDA shortly before the war, and were you heavily involved in the formation of that political party, and indeed did you become mayor of Brcko in the 1990 election?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC
utterances.text: Yes. Everything that you have said is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Before we turn to matters of detail with which you can assist the Tribunal, I'm going to ask you to help them with three maps, if the usher would be so good.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The order I'm going to present them is the small one first, the green one second, and the town map third. The small one, therefore, becomes exhibit number --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: If a copy of that can go on the ELMO, as this is a public hearing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Does this map show the division of Bosnia-Herzegovina as between the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina and the Republic of Srpska?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC
utterances.text: Yes, it does.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Does it show the position of Brcko at an extremely narrow part of what is the Republika Srpska, linking the eastern to the western parts of that body?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC
utterances.text: Yes. That's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The significance of that area of land on which Brcko fell being obvious, for it's the only connecting point between the eastern and the western parts?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC
utterances.text: Yes. That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The second map, please, will be the green map, which, I imagine, becomes Exhibit 57.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Your Honour, the Defence doesn't have any copies of these items.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm so sorry. I've provided enough copies for the registrar to distribute them. By being efficient in that way, I'd overlooked the Defence interest. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This map shows Brcko, and it's a little hard to see on the displays but -- thank you very much. It's towards the right of what is on the screen. First of all, we can see, can we not --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: First of all, we can see, Mr. Ramic, that Brcko lies on the south of the River Sava. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that the River Sava itself marks the border between what and what at this part of the land?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC
utterances.text: Marks the border between Bosnia-Herzegovina and the neighbouring state of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: If the technical staff would be good enough to come back just a little further from the part of the map that they've highlighted. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can we see Bjeljina -- a bit further still, please. Thank you -- now in the bottom right-hand corner of the map. Above that can we see Batkovic?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC
utterances.text: Yes, you can.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Other places that may have been referred to in the evidence can always be identified later.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: May the witness have the next map, please, will become Exhibit 58. It has with it a key. The map is a little large for the ELMO, but for the purposes of the public, if the witness could have the pointer; although the Chamber may find it more convenient to follow it with the key on the original copies of the maps they have.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can we see, Mr. Ramic, on this map, towards the north-west, marked number 1, the hospital, with the health centre on the opposite side of the road and the wooden mosque next door to it?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC
utterances.text: Yes. That's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Following that road round, are there three more mosques, 4 and 5, and I myself can't -- and then 6, the middle of the point on the west. Four and 5, and then 6 down there is another mosque. Going back towards the top of the map is number 7, the SUP building, in the centre of town. The nearness or otherwise of the SUP building from the Luka warehouse facility can be seen on the map. Could you just point out Luka facility to us, please? The Chamber, I think, knows where it is.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC
utterances.text: [Indicates]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's it. It's the black buildings lining the side of the River Sava. Number 8 is the Partizan Sports Hall, number 9 the JNA barracks. Then if we come down further on the map, on the roads running south -- and there are two roads running south -- if you take the road that runs almost due south, it goes to a place marked 10, and was that the Laser Bus Company?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC
utterances.text: Yes. That's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you take the road that runs, I suppose, south/south-east, does that road come to somewhere marked 12, and then beyond that to somewhere marked 11? Can you see the markings 12 and 11?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC
utterances.text: I pointed to them. This is 11 and that's 12 [indicates].

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, although you may not have been back after the war at any time when you could see where mass grave sites were found, is it your understanding -- and there will be further evidence of this to assist the Chamber, but is it your understanding that 12 is the approximate area of the mass grave sites?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And Number 11 is some farms.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC
utterances.text: Farms, yes. Those are the farms there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. I'll now turn to the detail of your evidence. Before I do so, have you seen a summary of your evidence? Have you seen a summary of your evidence, which is now being produced to you?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC
utterances.text: I've got it, yes, I've seen it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And subject to amendments that were made when you were first here in The Hague, is that document correct?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC
utterances.text: Yes, it's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In 1990, did you and your brother attend the first official meeting of the SDA in Sarajevo, becoming party members and campaigning strongly during that period of time in the Brcko municipality?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were your aims to include -- or were your aims to ensure democratic representation for Bosniaks, they being the majority ethnic group at that time?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC
utterances.text: That's right, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In paragraph 3 of your summary, a number of statistics are set out. Were they provided by you, or alternatively provided to you and checked by you some time ago?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC
utterances.text: I provided these figures, and they are absolutely correct and common knowledge.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The various statistics will not help to be read out, but if it comes to this, that when combining the Bosniak portion of the population with Yugoslavs, or people identified as Yugoslavs but also Bosniaks, was the proportion of Bosniaks as defined in that way something in the region of 53 per cent?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The proportion of people simply declared as Bosniaks being approximately 44 per cent?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC
utterances.text: 44? I think ,5 per cent, 44,5 per cent, exactly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You, with your brother, formed bodies called the municipal board and the executive board of the SDA, and people were elected to those bodies from local boards within the municipality, but there were also party members who hold no office; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And to paragraph 5: There were some 20 to 23 local boards in and around the municipality of Brcko, each having its own officers elected by local members?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC
utterances.text: That is correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You set out in paragraph 6 and 7 certain other details of the boards, which I needn't trouble you with at the moment, and we come to paragraph 8. At the time of the election in 1990, did the municipal parliament of Brcko consist of 90 seats, and did each contesting party put forward 90 nominations?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I now produce a compendious exhibit which comes in a plastic folder and will, I think, become compendiously Exhibit 59?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Prosecution Exhibit 59.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And if we keep the pages in the same order, we'll be able to run through them quite swiftly, and I hope efficiently.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The first page of Exhibit 59 is marked "A" in the top right-hand corner and is a list of 90 names. What are these names, please, Mr. Ramic?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC
utterances.text: It is a list of 90 candidates which the SDA party put forward for the general elections in 1990.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We see that you have highlighted numbers 6, 16, 23, 29, and 60, the significance of the highlights being ... ?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC
utterances.text: Those were individuals who, in my opinion, are not living today. They were killed in the war.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Following that election in 1990, did the SDP or Communist Party win the majority of the seats; namely, 24: the SDA coming second with 23, the HDZ gaining 21 seats, and the SDS winning but 14 seats?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC
utterances.text: Quite correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you turn to the second document, or second part of the overall document, headed "B" in the top right-hand corner and running to three sheets, I think, is this a list of the names with the party affiliations of those elected to the municipal parliament? And we can simply see the distribution of -- if we look in the brackets, SDP, Bosniak, Serb, Croat, Serb, Bosniak, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then that list goes over for various -- well, it goes over for the three pages, but what I was reading out on the first part was those who were under the banner of the SDP, and they are of various ethnic groupings. When you come to the bottom of the first sheet and to the SDA, they are, of course, all Bosniak. When you come to the second sheet, the HDZ, they were all Croats. And when you come to the third sheet, to the SDS, they are all Serbs. And you've made then reference to the "Reformisti" coalition with some six names, and just explain that for us, please.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC
utterances.text: That's how it was. SDP, the Communist Party, won 24 seats in the election, and this is the list of those persons who were elected and who represented members of the municipal parliament. So this was a mixed group; that is, there were Bosniaks, Serbs, and Croats. Next came the Party for Democratic Action, SDA, which won 23 seats, and here you have enclosed a list of those people who became members, council members. They were all Bosniaks. Then came the Croat Democratic Community, HDZ, which won 21 seats, and here is their list of those who became municipal councilmen, and they are all Croats. Then came the Serb Democratic Party, or SDS, which won 14 seats, and these are some of the municipal councilmen. Then the "Reformisti" coalition of reformists, who won six seats, and as you can see, they include both Bosniaks and Serbs, and these are the names of municipal councilmen elected then. Then the Muslim Bosniak organisation, MBO, which won one seat, and this is the name of that person. He is a Bosniak, and he was elected a councilman. And finally the Green Party, which won one seat, and that man was of Serb origin. He was also a municipal councilman.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The next document, please, and it may be helpful, although the witness doesn't necessarily refer to it, it may be helpful to the public if we provide a spare copy of these documents, and then they can go on the ELMO for the public to see. And we're now up to the document, about page 4, I think, marked "C," and while we are looking at that, just checking that the right one comes on the ELMO. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is this a diagrammatic representation of the structure within the Brcko municipality?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In fact, I think what happened was, following the election, that the SDP and the SDA formed a coalition with the HDZ and the SDS, and in that coalition, the SDA did hold the majority; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC
utterances.text: I think that this is not quite correct. After the election, the coalition at the level of the state of Bosnia-Herzegovina was set up by the SDA, HDZ, and SDS, in order to take over the power, and the same happened in the municipality of Brcko. It is not correct that the SDA had the majority, because all three parties in the government in power shared the power. It was more or less a parity, a relationship on par.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If we look at the diagram, the president, who had a vice-president, the president was whom? You?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You show that underneath your vice-president, there was the parliament, and then below that -- I'm sorry this isn't in translation -- the next body immediately below that is what body?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC
utterances.text: That is the municipal government. What it says here is the executive board or the executive council.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that comprised three SDA, three Croatian, and three Serbian members?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Going further up -- I'll come to the bottom of the drawing in a minute, but if we go further up again, apart from the secretarial support, we see on the left the police; we see on the right the Territorial Defence.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then to the right of the Territorial Defence, we see -- what's that there? SU --

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC
utterances.text: This is the court. This is the court.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And in each case you've drawn a line going directly up to a minister -- to the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, or to a minister or ministry in the republic. Can you just explain what that represents?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC
utterances.text: The court which I'm showing was directly subordinated to the Ministry of the State of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Then the Territorial Defence, which I'm pointing at now [indicates], was subordinate to the republican headquarters of the State of Bosnia-Herzegovina, so that was the republican Territorial Defence headquarters. The police here was directly under the ministry of the police of Bosnia-Herzegovina, so those were autonomous structures which were not accountable to me, or rather to municipal authorities.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Looking at the bottom of the picture, which will need a marginal adjustment -- thank you very much -- on the ELMO, have you here set out various ministries; for example, education and other functions?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me turn over to the next part of your exhibit, which is marked D.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC
utterances.text: This is the diagram of the graph of the municipal government, with all of the municipal ministries.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm just going to interrupt to say this: I'm very grateful to my case manager. With her usual efficiency, she draws to my attention that there are French translation available for nearly all of this document. One or two of the last annexes haven't yet been translated into French, but the balance of the document is available, if that would assist the Tribunal. It may be that there are a sufficiently limited number of words in either English or French that the Chamber's happy to continue without them, but they're here if required. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Thank you. All these explanations are very clear, but we are really very happy to also have the French version. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The next document, D, is really a repetition of the previous document with the parliament now -- the picture of the intervening parliament cut out. What you've done on this diagram is not only identify certain post holders, but you've also identified their ethnic origins or groupings. So we see here that the president is marked as -- not as you but as Pero Markovic. Can you just explain that?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC
utterances.text: This graph here shows the municipal government, which is made on a parity level, as I've already said. That is, nine members altogether; three were Bosniaks, three were Serbs, and three were Croats. The president of the government -- that is, the Prime Minister -- was a Serb, and I'm showing, now pointing at his name, Pero Markovic [indicates]. He was a Serb. His deputy was Munib Jusufovic, a Bosniak. Then you have number 3, which is the Ministry for Revenue, for the budget, for taxes, and the head of that Ministry was a Croat. It's this box here [indicates] --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We need not go through --

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC
utterances.text: -- and so on and so forth, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Again, the distribution amongst the ethnic groupings is revealed. Thank you. We can now go to, I think, the next document, which is marked E, and there's only one sheet. Just explain this for us, because it may be being looked at in translation, but if you could explain it for us, please, very briefly.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC
utterances.text: This here is a document showing how the municipal power was distributed on a parity basis, as I have just mentioned -- the significance, the ranking, the character of functions -- so that here, under 1, we have three posts, which are the highest-ranking posts at the municipal level.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: There is your name as the president?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC
utterances.text: Yes. First comes the president, the mayor. Yes. That is me, yes. Then the next name. This is the Prime Minister. That is the president of the government, and that is Pero Markovic, a Serb. Then third ranking is the head of the local police, Stjepan Filipovic, a Croat.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Then we've just -- we needn't go beyond, I think. Beside number 2, what does the title beside number 2 tell us?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC
utterances.text: Number 2, it repeats the diagram which you just saw; that is, the government, the composition of the government.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And number 3?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC
utterances.text: Number 3. Number 3 -- number 3 is my deputy -- that is, deputy mayor -- and he is a Croat.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Over then to document F, which we can see from the heading is the territorial -- the police at the top, and the Territorial Defence two-thirds of the way down, and again you've identified various post holders. It can all be gone into detail if required, but does it again show a distribution of jobs between the various parties and indeed between the various ethnic groups?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC
utterances.text: So this document shows, first, the structure of the police, I mean the ethnic composition of the police, and the distribution of different duties of different posts in the police. So on the one -- and says "Police." Then the topmost post is the head, head of the police, and that was a Croat, Stjepan Filipovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC
utterances.text: Then comes the commander of policemen, and that was a Serb, Mitar Milic. The third one is the head of inspection services, and it was this one, Tanjic, and he was a Bosniak. Below that, here, we have an approximate ethnic structure of the police; that is, there were about 55 per cent of Serbs, 27 per cent were Bosniaks, and Croats were about -- amounted for about 18 per cent. So this was the state of affairs that I found when I came to -- when I became the mayor.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Then the Territorial Defence has been dealt with in a similar way and the distribution is revealed.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC
utterances.text: Yes. Identical.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Over to the following page marked G. This is the schools in the municipality, with their directors shown and their ethnic categorisation: Serb, Bosniak, and one Croat shown, I think, as the director of the listed schools.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At the bottom of the page --

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: -- the director of the schools: 9, 2, and 1. I think that's what I've already dealt with.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC
utterances.text: Yes. That is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. We will return to the exhibit shortly, and I'll take you to the 1st of May of 1992. Before the events of the 1st of May, 1992, had you had warnings of things to come both from individuals and from things that you could see yourself?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC
utterances.text: There were many signs and rumours that something was in the offing, that something -- that a bloodshed might occur. There were all sorts of events, all sorts of indicators, beginning from the general state of affairs in Bosnia-Herzegovina which prevailed during the latest period of time, which, of course, affected the municipality of Brcko. There were also various signs of what was coming in the municipality itself, including direct calls to me by individual citizens, either by those who were trying to tell me about these things openly or surreptitiously, and the behaviour of the army was particularly symptomatic. I think it most struck the ire. It was quite evident that the army was getting ready, or, rather, the army was involved in whatever was about to happen. There is a great deal of evidence about that. I could really spend a lot of time telling you about it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Summarising it as you have done in paragraph 16, or has been done for you in paragraph 16, did you become aware of the gathering of military equipment and soldiers, the distribution of weapons to Serb villages in the municipality, building of roadblocks and checkpoints, and also the presence of paramilitary groups in and around the town?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC
utterances.text: Yes. As I have said, it lasted for several months before the war broke out. The army was distributing the weapons among the Serb population in villages. Then the army had also involved the reserve troops, and they were made up exclusively of Serbs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right. As to the men you saw in and around the town, were you aware of men foreign to the area; and if so, what sort of numbers and what sort of ages? Don't read the summary, because I think if you just tell the Judges, it will be more helpful. Were you aware of men foreign to the area; and if so, what sort of numbers and what sort of age were they?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC
utterances.text: It was quite obvious. So for about a month or two before the war, in the town of Brcko there were about 300 or even 400 men, that sort of magnitude, who were not from the area, whom we did not know. So they were outsiders. They were mostly aged between 20 to, say, 35.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you inquire -- paragraph 17, but you don't trouble with that yourself, Mr. Ramic -- but did you inquire of the JNA commander what was happening and did he tell you?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC
utterances.text: I would -- I called him repeatedly in relation to all these happenings, and on several occasions I also went to see him and talk to him and ask him why all these activities, and particularly why were the tanks digging in and why were groups with machine-guns deployed around the town or on the main roads. What was particularly odd was that most of these weapons were aimed at the town. He would not discuss it much and, as a rule, would reply to all my questions that it was in line with some army activities. Or when I would be very direct and very blunt, then he would answer, "I don't have to answer that."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he in any way explain the build-up of forces by reference to any threat from elsewhere?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC
utterances.text: From time to time he would answer that these activities were being conducted also as a defence against incursion of some foreign forces. When I would ask him, "What important forces?" then he would say, "From Croatia." Should I continue?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If there's anything more to fill out that answer, yes, anything else that he said to you that's --

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC
utterances.text: Yes. So he seemed to be concerned about the safety of the citizens there, thinking that they might -- that it might be imperilled by the incursion of some forces from outside, and by that he meant Croatia. On that occasion, I told him, "Well, if this is the concern for the citizenry, then why don't we organise a joint unit?" That was my proposal for him: 150 men strong, with 50 Serbs, 50 Croats, and 50 Bosniaks, and let them look after the area and be placed under his command. However, he refused that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did the SDS, the party of the Serbs, make a claim to divide Brcko, a claim which was initially unacceptable to your party, not least because of your majority or comparative majority position in the town?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC
utterances.text: The SDS did not have a majority in the town, by no means. The overall number of -- they accounted for barely 20 per cent of the population in the town, and even in the territory of the municipality of Brcko, the Serb population again accounted for some 20 per cent. But they wanted to divide it, to partition the town, and they were saying -- they were doing it quite openly, because they wanted to call it the Serb Municipality of Brcko.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Under the pressure that you were facing, was there a televised parliamentary session on the 27th of April, where the SDA's proposition to divide the town was debated?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC
utterances.text: Well, these requests to have the town divided, to have a Serb Municipality of Brcko established, that was something that we could not accept because it was impossible. I mean, it was simply not feasible. Of course, we were not particularly happy to be involved in such discussions. But then they began to threaten and said, "Well, if you won't do it, then we shall do it by force." At that, we agreed to convene the parliament -- rather, the municipal parliament -- and have a decision about that. That was on the 17th of April, 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The result of the debate was what?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC
utterances.text: Well, I have to say that all the parties in the town took part in it. It was very tense. In other parts of Bosnia-Herzegovina, people were already being killed. The war was already on. Even in the neighbourhood community -- in the adjacent community -- even in the neighbouring community of Bjeljina, for instance, it had already broken out. So people were sensing that, and they were afraid that the same thing might happen in Brcko, and then they accepted -- and then they accepted -- they agreed then to have the municipality divided. So the conclusion of that parliamentary debate was to allow them to take out a part of the town and part of the municipality and call it the Serb Municipality of Brcko. However, at that time, we did not determine -- we did not define that particular part and when it would go into force. We had decided to do that at the next session, which was called for the 4th of May.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Between --

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC
utterances.text: I should like to adjust one more thing. So it was as early as April -- I'm referring to the SDS. So in early April, before all that I'm talking about had happened, they had already proclaimed the Serb Municipality of Brcko through some decisions that they had taken, and they also had it carried by various media. So we knew that they had already decided that they would be a Serb Municipality of Brcko, and they had even decided who would be the mayor of their municipality, and his name was Djordje Ristanic, and he was one of the SDS councilmen in our parliament.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Between -- well, at around this time, but between the date of the discussion or debate on television and the 1st of May, when the bridges were blown up, were people leaving Brcko for safer territory?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC
utterances.text: Yes. This was very noticeable. Many people were leaving the town, and sometimes there was a sort of panic situation because many, many people were leaving.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Indeed, did there come a time when your own family left but you stayed?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC
utterances.text: Yes. Let me add that my mother, who was old, was ailing. She lived with me. I had small children. My son was only six years old at the time, and so I had to take care of them too, but it was only five or six days before the outbreak of war.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Can we return to map Exhibit 57, please, which is the green map; this one. It shows the geography in some detail. It isn't in the summary, but I think the witness may be able to help with this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: By the 1st of May, when the bridges over the Sava at Brcko were blown up, where was the nearest effective bridge east or west of Brcko, and had any other bridges by then been destroyed, please?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC
utterances.text: On the 1st of May, when the bridges in Brcko were destroyed, there was not a single bridge across which you could go to Croatia. All the bridges had already been destroyed. Otherwise, the nearest bridge, which was destroyed several months previously, was in Orasje, which is about 20 kilometres away from Brcko, 25 kilometres.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you saying that for the total length of this map, all the way west past Bosanski Brod and past Bosanski Gradica, there were no bridges --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, Mr. Nice, please. We didn't hear you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm sorry. My mistake.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you saying that on this map, going west past Bosanski Brod and all the way through Bosanski Gradiska, there were no bridges at the time that the bridge at Brcko was blown up?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC
utterances.text: That's right. There was not a single bridge you could go across. There were bridges, but they had all been destroyed previously.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We know from other evidence that when the bridges at Brcko were blown up, many people were killed and their body parts found in and around the town. And again, this is not something that's covered in your summary, but I'm going to ask you to deal with it in any event. Two parts to the question. First, how did it come about that there were people on the bridge liable to be killed in that way? And the second part of the question: Can you help us, from what you may now know, about whether any Serbs were killed in that destruction, or not; and if not, why not?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC
utterances.text: First of all, I'd like to say that we were afraid that somebody might blow up the bridge, and so I ordered the bridge to be protected. A group of policemen was set up, a sort of control point, checkpoint, at the bridge itself. This checkpoint was manned by ten individuals, so that the bridge could not be destroyed by anybody; it could only have been taken over and destroyed by a very well-prepared group of professionals. And that is in fact what happened. Later on, we learnt from the survivors -- that is to say, from the policemen who had protected the bridge -- that in the course of the night, a group of some 20 men turned up. That is what the professional policemen told us, that they saw another very well-prepared group of people, numbering some 20 individuals, and that most of those people spoke a dialect which showed that they had come from Serbia. And they had taken over our checkpoint. They brought in a vehicle full of dynamite. This was ascertained later on, because the policemen had seen that they brought a vehicle up and placed it at the end of the bridge and waited to activate the explosive. All this is correct, and we have the testimonies of witnesses, eyewitnesses. And then they waited for the morning, which is to say the 30th of April, at 4.30 a.m., to activate the explosive. The reason for which they waited was that as there was a situation of war in Croatia, Croatia did not allow free passage across the bridge. However, at intervals, at a certain time, it would allow people to pass across, so that an agreement had been reached that they should give free passage to people between 4.00 and 5.00 a.m., and that is the time when they would allow people to pass across from Croatia into Bosnia-Herzegovina. There were many men from Bosnia-Herzegovina who were employed in Croatia and Slovenia, Germany, Austria; that is to say, the neighbouring western countries. And that is -- the German term used is the gastarbeiters, the guest workers. And they would come to visit their families, for two reasons. They would come first because at that time, there were the 1st of May celebrations, when they had their May Day holidays, and so they would take the weekend off; and on the other hand, their families informed them that the situation was very tense, and that they did not feel secure, so these people, these workers, wanted to go back home to protect their families. They were, for the most part, men; very active men, working men, aged between, say, 20 to 40. At that time, according to our later assessment, there were about 150 people on the bridge, and we're quite certain that there was not a single Serb amongst them. From what we learned later on, and the names of the people, as far as we were able to discover, all the names, all the people were in fact Bosniaks.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When the bridge was blown, were you in Brcko yourself?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you make an attempt with the local JNA commander not to have the town occupied by JNA troops but to let the civilian police maintain law and order, and did you indeed go on television seeking to calm the civil population?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC
utterances.text: Yes. Let me put it this way: You didn't ask me, but it is important to know that two bridges were blown up in Brcko. There were in fact two bridges. One was the one that we're discussing now, and that was the bridge and the -- both communication for vehicles and for pedestrians; and another one, a kilometre lower down, and that was a railway bridge, and that bridge too was blown up, within the space of three minutes, one after the other. The blowing-up of the bridge had the effect of being an exceptional catastrophe at that point, and it was very frightening, and panic reigned in town. Of course the people started to flee from their houses en masse, and they went towards the south, the south-lying regions. In this general panic, we had to deal with law and order in town, and I, myself, as the mayor, immediately convened a meeting of the defence council; according to my mandate, it was my duty to do so. A member of that body was commander of the garrison. However, he didn't wish to come to me, but he asked me to go to him, to the barracks. And I did this, although I knew that my safety would not be guaranteed. So I went to the meeting at the barracks, and I asked -- that is to say, he said that he would bring the army into town to take control of all the more important points in town. I think he told me this because he was not certain what would happen in town afterwards. He could have done that without telling me, in fact, but that was the reason; he wasn't sure, he didn't know what the army would encounter once they entered town. And at the time, I told him that I would not allow the army to enter into the town, that that was the job of the police force, and that it was up to the police to maintain law and order in town.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was it following that that you went on television?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC
utterances.text: Yes. When I said what I did, he put an ultimatum to me; that is, he laid down conditions. He said that if I succeeded in calming the population, and I would only be able to do so -- that was his request, that I go on local television and call upon the people to calm down. If I were to do this, then he would agree not to bring the army into town. And I accepted that. I accepted going on television and addressing the people.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the course of your time at the television station, did somebody telephone in to that television station with some news?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC
utterances.text: Yes. The programme lasted for a very short space of time. It lasted two or three minutes; not more than that. As soon as I appealed to the civilian population with instructions telling them not to panic, and that we would keep things under control, and so on, people called me up directly in the studio from various parts of town telling me that the army was already entering town. And then, at one point, people phoned me up directly from the local community of the 4th of July -- you have that in your documents -- and they let me know, "Well, Mr. President, the army is at present shooting at us." After that -- and this was all live, televised live -- the deputy commander of the garrison, who had come to the television station with me, I told him -- that is to say, I asked him, "Well, what does that mean? What's the army doing? Didn't we agree that the army was not to enter town?" And that is where the television programme was interrupted.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you decide that what had been said to you by the JNA commander was something you could not rely on anymore; and in consequence, did you, yourself, escape when you were able?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC
utterances.text: I think, and I claim that today, they didn't want to let me go; they would have kept me and probably killed me. And I bear this out by the fact that when we set out for the television station, which is in the centre of town, I was escorted by two armoured vehicles, with at least 20 well-armed individuals wearing different military uniforms. And they were very strange; they appeared very strange at the time. I didn't recognise them. And I in fact realised that I was their prisoner. But I wanted to save the people and the town, so I continued -- I kept my part of the bargain, kept my promise. And in the television station, after citizens had telephoned direct to say that the shooting had started, I took advantage of that interruption in the broadcast, and the commander -- when the commander didn't know what to do, having heard the news, what he did in fact was to try to check whether this was true, so I took advantage of that particular moment to leave the television studio, and luckily my own car was parked there, so I was able to get into my car and to escape their control.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You ultimately, as you say in your summary, went to a place which I think -- is it also called Free Brcko, or was it called Free Brcko, Gornji Rahic, and you were there for the war? Are we able to see that on the green map, or would it be the town map that would be most useful?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC
utterances.text: Yes, you can see it on the green map. Gornji Rahic is not marked there, but it is between these two places: Brka and Moaca. Right here, where I'm pointing at [indicates].

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... shows that it was possible to survive for the duration of the war, and that's where you were?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC
utterances.text: According to the law and my own mandate, in case of war or the imminent danger of war, I was head of the defence council; that was according to my mandate. And when the shooting started and the attack was launched by these units and paramilitary units, I organised the defence of the rest of the town, because -- we succeeded in controlling part of the town and the southern reaches. So we were able, in the course of the war, to do that, and I spent most of my time during the war there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'd like you now to return to the documentary exhibits, and if the usher would be good enough to carry on with the process of laying them on the ELMO for the advantage of the public while the witness looks at them on the desk in front of him, we've reached Annex H, which is a document with which the Chamber may already be familiar, three sheets of paper with 39 names typed on them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is this a list that you were asked to draw up, or that you certainly did draw up?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right; that's the list.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you asked to draw it up, or did you draw it up on your own initiative?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC
utterances.text: When we discussed these matters, I cannot remember whether I was asked to do so or whether I did it on my own, but I compiled the list, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This is 39 names of what exactly?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC
utterances.text: Those are the names of prominent citizens from Brcko, well-known citizens or prominent members of the SDA party who were killed, whom I know were killed on the first day of the conflict or aggression.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: If the Chamber, as it were, keep its hand on Exhibit H, or Annex H, and if the witness would be good enough then to turn over to the next document, which is headed I, and which runs to some six pages of names, a hundred in all, the Chamber will want to know that it's looking at a document that is not in alphabetical order; that is, document I is not in alphabetical order, but it is a hundred names, and it is subject to one correction. It is -- certainly at least one correction. It is the same hundred names as the Chamber has been looking at on Exhibit 12, where the names have been re-ordered into an alphabetical list, but at the time that this witness saw this list, for general reference only, it was in this format; that is to say, it was not alphabetical.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So, Mr. Ramic, were you shown the document I've just spoken of to the Chamber; namely, the document headed I, of a hundred names?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC
utterances.text: Yes, I was shown the document.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you asked on that document to identify, by highlighting, witnesses -- names that you knew as being either prominent or, if not prominent, at least associated with the SDA?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, that was it, more or less. They were either members of the party or sympathisers of the party or people who voted for the SDA party in the election.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If we stay with the first page of this Annex I and look at number 4, where the name "Amer Jasarevic" was written down, there was a correction. Is that your correction or somebody's correction before the document came to you, to "Enes"?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC
utterances.text: Yes. On the list that I was shown, it said "Amer Jasarevic". However, that was not correct. His real name was Enes Jasarevic. He was a man for -- whom we know was killed in Brcko during that time. He has a son called Amer, who is alive today.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As the Chamber can discover, the witness has highlighted, from this list of 100 names, some 57 associated, in the way he's described, with the SDA. If we move on from Annex I to Annex J, please. It's the next sheet in the bundle, please, Mr. Ramic. I think it will be underneath. Here's another copy coming, to save time. Is this a document prepared by you that shows the local SDA boards?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC
utterances.text: Yes. I did that, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell us about the particular areas you've highlighted in blue here. One of them -- for example, Kolobara -- is probably familiar to the Chamber as an essentially or a Muslim-dominated area. Tell us about the others and tell us what you've highlighted.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC
utterances.text: This shows a diagram of the organisation of the SDA party at the level of the Brcko municipality, and these rectangles here contain the names of the local branches of the party, who were linked up with areas in town or with villages in the Brcko municipality. Down here you have the villages, and up here is the town proper. Down below are the villages. So part of the town -- as you can see, Kolobara here, the next Gluhakovac, Mujkici, et cetera, and the blue designates those sections of town which were occupied on the 1st of May and where the killings took place.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The areas that you've highlighted, were some or all of them areas with a Muslim majority population?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC
utterances.text: All the areas were majority ones, with the exception of this one here, Grcica, the first one. There was a majority Serb population, whereas the other areas were Bosniak for the most part.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And all occupied on that 1st of May?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC
utterances.text: Yes. That's right. They were all occupied on the 1st of May.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Next document, please, Annex K. Again, we can see some familiar names now. In particular, we start off with Kolobara. What can you tell us about this list? First of all, before we come to the highlightings in two different colours, blue and yellow, what are the handwritten names, area by area?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC
utterances.text: They are the composition of the local councils of the SDA party. So each of these local sort of cells, organisations of the SDA, consisted of a Local Board with five members, and those are the names of the members in the areas which were occupied straightaway on the 1st of May and where the killings took place. So we have Kolobara first, Bijeljinska Cesta, Novo Brcko.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The highlightings in blue show what, if you can remember?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC
utterances.text: Blue denotes the people who were killed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is this the names that -- is this names that you found on -- the hundred names on the list?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC
utterances.text: Yes. A part of it. Not all the names. Not all the names are there, but most of them, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The yellow highlights, we see two on the first page --

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC
utterances.text: Yes. They're not on the list of 100 names, but they too were killed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And your knowledge that they were killed comes from other sources, does it?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC
utterances.text: In fact, we know that some people were killed in that way because there were eyewitnesses to the killings. There were witnesses who carried their dead bodies as well, and we also have cases where there are no witnesses, where the people have disappeared, but no trace has yet been found of them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Finally, there is a last document. I think it's the last thing I have to ask the witness to deal with. It's also called I, because it's the same list of a hundred names, but it's now been highlighted in both blue, as original, and green. The green highlights refer to what?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC
utterances.text: The green colour denotes the names of people who later on -- that is to say, I saw this list on two occasions. The first time I recognised the names marked in blue. The second time, on the second occasion, I added these two other names marked in green. Today I can tell you that there are some other names which I recognise from this list which I have not marked in any way on the list.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The ones that you marked in green, were those names of people known to be associated with the SDA in the local communities and so on, the Local Boards?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC
utterances.text: Yes. Those are the same names.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Since there are 6 green names in addition to the 57 blue, that takes us to a total of 63 the number of names from the list of 100 that had a connection with the SDA. I don't know what you're going to tell me about the other names that you say you can now identify. Are you simply identifying names whose fate you know, or are you identifying names whose fate you know and you're able to say they're connected to the SDA?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC
utterances.text: This whole list -- and I can state my opinion on that -- has a common denominator, and that is that most of the names were linked up with the SDA.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. The other names that you wanted to tell me about, or you wanted to tell the Chamber about, but you said weren't marked but that you knew something about them, just take one of those names and give us an example of what it was you were going to tell us.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC
utterances.text: Well, I'll tell you in just a minute. For example, I'm looking at the name under number 33, Rasim Causevic. For example, that is the brother of a friend of mine, a prominent member of the SDA party. When I looked at the list the first time, I didn't recognise that name. Then, for example, there is number 61, Muharem Ahmetovic. That is the father of a policeman from Brcko; that is to say, I'm not speaking about that policeman, but I'm speaking about this particular man who voted for the SDA, and that was common knowledge, that he had voted for the party. I have other cases of this. For example, 86, Andrija Kolar. He's a Croat by ethnicity but married to a Muslim, and he was a policeman before the war. He too was killed, together with his son, because, if I can put it that way, he was, in a way -- I can't say he was a member of the SDA, but he was a sympathiser of the party. So that's how it goes. I could give you some other names as well. So I think that I could find other names and other cases in point.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: With the Chamber's leave and without being impertinent, it may be the time the Chamber was going to have a break, and if by chance it was --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Do you have many questions here or have you completed now?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I've completed the questions, but it looks like the witness might want one more opportunity to look through this list, and he might possibly come back after the break and give us details of any other names, because we know the Defence wants to know as much about these people as they can hear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. All right. We shall now adjourn and we shall resume at 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Tribunal is in session. Will you have the accused brought in, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, we shall resume.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Ramic, you were looking through that last list appendixed within your exhibit to see if there were other names you could help us with. Using the numbers on the left-hand side, if there were any other names that you could help us with, tell us what you've been able to find.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC
utterances.text: Please, would the Court allow me to raise an objection in relation to this list? I think that quite a few of these names are wrong, you see. And sometimes it's very hard to tell, and then when you look at the list for a longer period of time, then you think of the right name. But I think that quite a few of these names are wrong. At any rate, I will tell you the names now. 33, as I mentioned, Rasim Causevic. 61, Muharem Ahmetovic. 74, Ferid Ibrahimovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What about him?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC
utterances.text: He and the next one, 76, Hilmija Cerimagic, they are men who lived in my neighbourhood, near my place. They were my neighbours. The first one, Number 74, he even had a nickname, "Major." And 77, Sefko Selmanovic, that is an elderly gentleman, and I recognised him as the father of a colleague of mine, an engineer. Then number 85, it says here "Eldin Salkovic," but that is incorrect. I remembered that there is a person called Elvedin Salkanovic; that's a young man who was also killed. Then I also mention 86, Andrija Kolar. Then I recognised these two, 88 and 89. They are two brothers, young men, Aldin and Amir Tursic. They, just like number 85, Elvedin Salkanovic, were young men, members of the youth organisation of the SDA. Numbers 94 and 95, Enver Residovic, and down there it only says "Residovic." I think that this relates to two women whose last name was Residovic. One of the women was younger, and the other one was older, and they were both killed at the very beginning. That's what I wish to say. Perhaps there could be even more of the kind, but I'm sorry, I recognise the names under numbers 3, 6, and 7, respectively, Omerasevic. I know their names. I know their names. They are from a part of Brcko which we call Ciganluk.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The people that you've named, were they Muslims, or were there other ethnicities involved? You've spoken of the one Croat, number 86 --

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC
utterances.text: There were other ethnic groups as well. There are individuals of that kind here, too.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you just point that out, so that we know who they are?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC
utterances.text: There is also Number 17, Franjo Vugrincic; he is a Croat. Then 21, Josip Lucic; he is another Croat. Then 36, Miroslav Kljukijevic; he is also a Croat. 45, Stipo Glavosevic; he is also a Croat. And as far as I can see, 86, Andrija Kolar; he is another Croat.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And as to their deaths, did you hear anything that explained why they were killed?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC
utterances.text: Yes. The one under 21, Josip Lucic, he was a young fellow, his nickname was Pepa, and it does say so here. He was a prominent athlete, a prominent sportsman in Brcko. And I know -- or rather, I have been informed from reliable sources that the accused had killed him, personally. Then 45, Stipo Glavosevic. He is a middle-aged man, and he was a butcher at the Bimeks meat factory in Brcko, and I was told by witnesses that he had also been killed by the accused personally. 86, Andrija Kolar, and here the name of his son is missing, and there are witnesses who saw him killed, too. As for the others, I've only heard that they have been killed, but about these, I know for certain that they were killed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... the reason why Andrija Kolar and his son were killed?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC
utterances.text: Andrija Kolar and his son, they were killed because -- I believe because -- it is difficult for me to explain it -- because they were people that Serbs did not trust much. They distrusted them because his wife was a Muslim and his grandfather was a Croat. His wife was a saleswoman, and she was an acquaintance of my family, if I may put it that way.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The other Croats who were killed, do you have any reason -- thank you for telling us who they were, but do you have any reasons for why they were killed?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC
utterances.text: I believe that the SDS policy, basically, was -- and one could really see that in many things, that it was -- that it was focusing on the elimination of other ethnic groups so as to gain areas in which they represented an absolute majority, ethnically speaking, I mean. A particular reason -- that is, those people had not done anything, so there was no other reason for that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Before I turn from the list -- and there's one other question I've got to get you to deal with, but on this long list of the names of those who were killed, is there anything about the distribution of professions or jobs amongst those you've been able to identify? Were they all working men, or were they all professional men, or was there an even distribution of occupations, or was there an emphasis on a particular type of occupation or position in society? Tell us.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC
utterances.text: We have a very diverse structure on this list. Some are very young and some are of fairly advanced age; that is, ranging between 20 to -- close to 70, I should say. And a very wide range of occupations. There were a number of prominent citizens, but also rank-and-file people, so there is hardly anything that they would all have in common. The only thing that they do have in common, I believe, is that the majority of them were nothing else than just the supporters of the SDA party.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Of course, when you marked your list of 39 names of the prominent Muslims, I think you identified -- was it some -- the list of 39 prominent names, was that names of people who you believed to be killed, or was it just 39 prominent names at the time?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC
utterances.text: No, this is a list of prominent persons who were killed and who belonged to -- prominent Bosniaks, ethnically.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I have been asked by Defence counsel to just deal with one other of the annexes. It's the one that comes immediately before the last list. It's got an "L" on it, and I passed over it rather quickly, having looked at "K," so it might be convenient if we just put "K" and "L" together. You've dealt with K and told us about how these people were representing the SDA in local communities and how the highlightings show those who have been killed. Just deal now with the similar document that is Annex L.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC
utterances.text: Document K originated in the course of a conversation which I had about half a year ago, several months ago, but at that time, I think that I didn't have enough time, as we talked, and I had no time to properly draw up this document, the L one. So I did that subsequently, because we then decided that I should provide the names of those 12 local boards which had been occupied. So the document L was something that I had promised to supply the Tribunal subsequently, and I wrote that subsequently. It shows other occupied parts of the town of Brcko, where the SDA party was and where those individuals were killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. That's all I ask of this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Now, as you know, Mr. Ramic, it is the Defence of the accused who will now take the floor and who will be asking the questions, which it is their right to ask. Will you tell us how long the examination-in-chief lasted?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: One hour and thirty minutes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. Mr. Greaves, you have more or less one hour and thirty minutes, perhaps a bit more than that. Do you think that will be enough?

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Possibly up to two hours, but I hope to finish today. That's what I'm aiming at.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. But we shall have another break because we have a long afternoon today. So we shall have another break. Mr. Greaves, you can begin. Cross-examined by Mr. Greaves:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Ramic, can I start by asking you to do this, please: If I ask you a question which you do not understand or which is confusing or badly asked, just stop me straightaway, ask me to repeat, and I'll do my best to make it a more sensible question. Is that all right? Mr. Ramic, can I ask you, please --

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC
utterances.text: Yes, quite all right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can I ask you, please, are you still involved in the political life of your country?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How long did your involvement in politics continue after the war in 1992?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC
utterances.text: In the latter half of -- until October 1993, I was the president of the wartime presidency of the municipality of Brcko; that is, in the area of the municipality of Brcko. Then I moved to Tuzla as a member of the government of the Tuzla district. In 1994, I became the president of the assembly of the parliament in the canton of Tuzla, and I was there until October 1996, and after that I did not want to be involved in politics any longer.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Before you became involved in forming the SDA and getting involved with that party in the Brcko area, had you been involved in any other political party before then, or was this something that for the first time you started to become involved in politics?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC
utterances.text: No. I was not actively involved in politics before that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the course of the time when you were involved in setting up and getting involved in things like elections and so on, did you become familiar with not just your own party, but the people who were involved in other political parties?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC
utterances.text: You mean locally?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Locally is what I'm principally interested in.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC
utterances.text: Yes, we knew one another.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you confirm this for me, Mr. Ramic: that prior to the war breaking out in 1992, Goran Jelisic was not involved with any political party or political movement in the Brcko area at all?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC
utterances.text: I wouldn't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you hear anything of him prior to the war, in any way at all, as being in the SDS or any of the other political parties?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC
utterances.text: No, I haven't heard about that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just to get the historical context precise, can you confirm this: that the order in which the various political -- new political parties emerged in the early 1990s was this: Firstly the SDA; then the HDZ; and finally, of the ethnically based parties, the SDS? Would that be correct?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC
utterances.text: Excuse me. Do you again mean at the local level?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At a republic level.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC
utterances.text: At the republic level, it is quite possible that such a list existed, but there was very little time because all the deadlines were very short.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And of the former regime, what we would commonly refer to as the Communist Party, that changed its identity somewhat, did it, and became the Social Democratic Party?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Of the fellow members of the Executive Board that was initially set up, of which your brother was the party president, is this right: that just one of those people, as far as you know, was killed, Smail Ribic?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is quite true; one of the members of the Executive Board.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just so that I understand it correctly, the system for election at which you and your party participated, was that by the preparation of a list for each party of 90 candidates, and the voting was done on the basis of the voter voting for the party, as a result of which then certain numbers of that party were then elected?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC
utterances.text: Yes. You could say that, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would that be depending on the number of votes that the party got in order -- when the list is submitted by the party, 1 to 90, if you get enough votes for 24 members, the first 24 names on the list would have been elected?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC
utterances.text: Yes, quite. One has to respect the sequence.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did all of the parties which contested that election, did they all advance 90 names? For example, as well as the principal parties who won seats, the Reform Coalition as well, the MBO, did they all put 90 names forward?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC
utterances.text: Yes. It was by statute like that. Any party which wanted to take part in the elections had to come up with a list of 90 names.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could I ask you, please, Mr. Ramic, to look at Annex B, if you'd be so kind? Before we turn and I start asking you specific questions about that list, can you help me about this: As well as your obvious interest in what the fate of your own party members and party members of parliament and so on were concerned, as the former mayor of Brcko, have you taken an interest over the years in the fate of other political parties, and members of other political parties, and members of parliament belonging to other political parties from Brcko?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC
utterances.text: Yes, but here I cannot -- or, rather, I could not learn the fate of SDS members.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Of course. I understand why that should be so, and I'm not going to ask you anything about the SDS. Let me just ask you, first of all, about the first party on Annex B, Mr. Ramic. We can see there that's the SDP, former Communist Party, 24 members. Of those who were elected, by my count it's 11 out of the 24 were Bosniaks. First of all, just to make it absolutely plain, is this right: that the word "Bosniak" is interchangeable with "Muslim"? Is that fair in this context?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC
utterances.text: Possibly so, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The figure I've just given you, 11 out of the 24, was that a similar proportion -- if you take the list of 90 who were put forward for election, would that proportion of Muslims or Bosniaks have been reflected as well in the list of 90, approximately half?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC
utterances.text: I think that it is approximately so, but take into account the proportion within the population. It was more in favour of the Bosniak population than what you have here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It may be that I'm being not very bright, but can you just explain that a little more? I don't understand it entirely. In what way was it more in favour of the Bosnian population -- the Bosniak population?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC
utterances.text: Well, if you look at the population of the municipality of Brcko, and I already mentioned this in the introduction, there were at least 53 per cent or perhaps even more. What we have here is a different ratio. Out of 24 there were 11 Bosniaks. That's not even 50 per cent.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I understand that, but it's not far off 50 per cent, is it, Mr. Ramic? And it's a small enough difference to be not very significant, I suggest.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you help us about this: Do you know of the fate of or continued existence of those members of that list from the SDP who are listed as Bosniak?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. I know the fate of most of them. Dzevdet Kurtalic, who was president of this party, is somewhere abroad. Number 5, Adem Ribic, spent the entirety of the war in the territory of the municipality of Brcko. He is from the village of Satorovici, which was not occupied, so he could remain there. Then 6, Ibrahim Vajzovic. He is from the town of Brcko, and I think that he is now in America. Seven, Hasim Muftic. He is from town. He was in the camp and was severely mistreated, but since he's an elderly man, we managed to exchange him. Then he died during the course of the war, as a consequence of the abuse in camp. Number 10 is Sabahet Drpljanin. He lives in Tuzla right now. Then number 14, Zekerijah Osmic. He is an MP in the parliament of that entity which is called Republika Srpska, and he lives in Tuzla. Then number 15, Jasminka Salkamovic. She is somewhere abroad. I don't know where, but she is not in Bosnia-Herzegovina. Sixteen, Hajrudin Ciric. He is also not in Bosnia-Herzegovina. I think he's in Germany. Number 18, Bajro Avdic. He was away throughout the war. Eighteen, Bajro Avdic. He is in Sarajevo right now, but during the war he was outside Bosnia-Herzegovina. Number 19, Nihad Mulalic. Throughout the war he was out of Bosnia-Herzegovina. He was not there. Number 21, Mustafa Nukovic. He is in the territory of the municipality of Brcko, and at present he is in the multi-ethnic authorities of the future district of Brcko. Number 22, Ferid Bijelic; and number 23, Muhamed Mujkamovic, both of them were abroad throughout the war. The one under number 22 returned a year ago, and 23 is still somewhere abroad.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So with one exception, number 7, Hasim Muftic, all of those are alive and well in some part of the world?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC
utterances.text: Yes. That is correct. However, you should bear in mind the fact that they managed to escape before the aggression against the town of Brcko took place; that is to say that they were not in Brcko during the aggression.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'd like to turn now, please, to the page which I think is numbered 8 in the top right-hand corner, Mr. Ramic, the Reformisti Koalicija. You'll forgive my poor pronunciation of your language.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Again, a political party that appears to have won six seats at that election; and of those six, five are listed as Bosniak. Is that a proper reflection of the list of 90 that that party advanced in terms of it's proportion?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC
utterances.text: I'm not competent in terms of explaining the composition of other parties, but if you want to hear my opinion, here it goes: This party had problems because Serbs did not want to join it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I understand that, but nevertheless, was it effectively dominated by Bosniaks?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC
utterances.text: They did not have any other composition but that one. It is only logical.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Of those names listed there, can you, as you have done with the list of the SDP, assist us as to the fate of those people?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC
utterances.text: Smajl Kurtalic, number 1, he was abroad. He was abroad throughout the war. Enes Pasalic was also abroad, but I think that he returned approximately two years ago and now he's in Bosnia-Herzegovina, in the territory of the municipality of Brcko. Number 3, Amir Muminovic.
