He was in the territory of the municipality of Brcko throughout the war. Number 4, Goran Trupl. Throughout the war he was in Brcko, and to the best of our knowledge, he was one of the commanders on the Serb side. Number 5, Izudin Karahmetovic, spent the entire war abroad, but about a year ago he returned. And Number 6, Zlatko Musanovic, was also abroad throughout the war, but he returned as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can we now turn, please, to the MBO, Muslim Bosnian organisation. Again, may we infer from its name that that was an ethnically based political party, political grouping?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC
utterances.text: Well, yes. That may be inferred.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the one name that we have there, Hamo Jerkovic, can you say anything of what happened to him?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC
utterances.text: Throughout the war, he was in the territory of the municipality of Brcko. But may I tell you straightaway that that is a sick man.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Of course, but he's alive and survived the war?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC
utterances.text: Yes, of course. But again, I repeat, he escaped, before the aggression, from town.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If I may say so, your knowledge of the people is reasonably encyclopaedic. Would you be able to repeat this exercise if you had the additional names of those who were not elected, from the lists of 90, for the SDP and the Reform Coalition and the MBO, as to what happened to them, if we were able to obtain it for you?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC
utterances.text: You have to know that I was president, president of the assembly, mayor of the town, and all these people were my MPs. And of course I knew them personally rather well, because before that, we worked together a year and a half before that, and I certainly know them better than those who were not members of parliament. So this is what I can say. I could give such answers for some other people, but not all, definitely.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right. Thank you. I'll return to the lists in due course, if I may, Mr. Ramic. I now want to ask you some questions about events in relation to the war. The war that broke out, effectively between the Serb population and the Muslim population, in May 1992, wasn't in fact the first, if I can call it, acts of serious violence of a military kind which had taken place in Brcko; there were other things that had happened in the immediate past. Would that be right?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC
utterances.text: You are probably referring to the fate of the Bosniaks in the history of Bosnia-Herzegovina. If that is what we are talking about, then I can say to you that Bosniaks in Bosnia and Herzegovina experienced similar genocides -- that's what I call them -- similar suffering in the past. There was no case of the reverse. History knows of no such example, that is to say that the Serbs ever suffered at the hands of the Bosniaks, throughout history.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I was rather thinking of an incident in 1991 when an ammunition train -- there was an attempt on an ammunition train by Croatian elements, an attempt to blow it up. That's what I was referring to. Do you recall that incident?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC
utterances.text: I don't know which incident you are referring to. I do not believe that that was of any significance; otherwise I would have remembered it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it also right that in March or April of 1992, a soldier in the uniform of the HVO was killed in Brcko, near to the SUP building?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC
utterances.text: Yes, that did happen, perhaps two months before the war. As far as I can remember, that man was not in an HVO uniform. I'm sure that he could not have had HVO insignia; that's for sure. But may I say immediately that he was killed by a man from the then-army; that is to say from the Brcko garrison.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can I now ask you, please, you've given some indication of the military buildup on the Serbian side, but is this not also right: that there were those elements on the Muslim side who were also engaged in procuring weapons for a future conflict at about that time?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC
utterances.text: I must admit that there were some people who illegally acquired weapons without official permission. However, you should know that at that time, there were some very difficult situations of aggression and bloodshed which all stemmed from the attacks by the army and the SDS; there were never any incidents the other way around. And it is quite understandable that some people, in fear, tried to obtain weapons for self-defence.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It was rather more than that, wasn't it, Mr. Ramic? There was a significant amount of attempts to procure military weapons, to arm militias, wasn't there?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC
utterances.text: We have to take facts into account, and the fact is that I, as mayor of Brcko, received direct information from the chief of police that the army was caught deploying weapons in Serb villages with army trucks, and we never received any such information the other way around, of providing weapons the other way around, never.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What about the Croatian Community? Were they arming themselves?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC
utterances.text: I think that they behaved in a similar way, and that individuals probably procured weapons in order to defend themselves.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'd like to ask you, please, about the callup of reservists to the former JNA. It's right, isn't it, that that callup was issued to all citizens regardless of their ethnic background?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC
utterances.text: You are probably referring to the summer of 1991. That is correct. However, I'd like to add one more thing to that, and that is that these reservists were called up with the intention of sending them to war in Croatia, against Croatia, and that is not what the people wanted. After that, when the people rebelled against this -- I have to add this -- the army no longer called up reservists from other ethnic groups, but Serbs exclusively, and the army turned into a uni-ethnic force.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, isn't it right, in fact, that the principal reason why people from the Muslim community didn't answer the summons was that they were encouraged not to do so by the leader of your party, Alija Izetbegovic?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC
utterances.text: I did not understand this. Who did Mr. Izetbegovic support?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It may be that I'm wrong, but did he not make a call for people to refuse the summons for callup? Wasn't that why Muslims in general refused to obey the summons?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC
utterances.text: I shall admit quite frankly that I do not recall that call, but I know full well that Muslims and Croats did not want to respond to callups as reservists because these people were sent to the front line in Croatia, to wage war against Croatia, and they didn't want to do that. That was the reason.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You've mentioned the existence of the garrison commander with whom you had dealings. What was the name of that gentleman?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC
utterances.text: His name was Pavle Milinkovic, and he was a lieutenant colonel.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And was it through his offices that you were able to establish the mixed patrols?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC
utterances.text: Mixed patrols existed throughout Bosnia-Herzegovina, and Brcko was no exception.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Perhaps you could just answer the question, please, Mr. Ramic: Was it through the garrison commander that you organised the patrols?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC
utterances.text: If you are referring to patrols in town, patrols in town, yes. But patrols outside town he did on his own. That is to say that the city was surrounded by army checkpoints.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And for how long or until what date did those patrols continue to be carried out?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC
utterances.text: Well, they were carried out formally until the very beginning of the war; that is to say, the 1st of May. However, during the last month -- that is to say, throughout April 1992 -- Serb policemen left these mixed patrols. They didn't want to be on them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'd like now just to turn, if we may, please, to the talks which took place over the division of Brcko with other political parties. Is this right, that those continued, really, right up until the very last minute?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC
utterances.text: Yes, one may say so. However, I must add that this was exclusively at my insistence.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's very commendable, that you should have continued to try and talk as long as possible. I don't want to go into the rights and wrongs of the argument, but there came a time, did there not, when the SDS was proving itself intransigent as to its position, and you and your colleagues decided to give in to some or all of their demands? Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC
utterances.text: They presented that kind of an ultimatum to us, and they threatened that they would resort to force if we did not meet their demands.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And those were essentially demands which -- again, I don't want to debate the rights and wrongs of them, but the demands were designed to give the Serbs a substantial part of Brcko, as it were, for their own?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC
utterances.text: They wanted to do something that had already been witnessed in other parts of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and that is to say, to establish territories under their own authority. I made an offer to them that we call the entire municipality of Brcko "the Serb municipality of Brcko", if that's what they wanted. However, that was not what they wanted. They wanted something in which they would be the only participants.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You, I suspect in common with a lot of your colleagues, became sufficiently concerned that you sent members of your family away from Brcko. Was that something which was generally the case in the SDA throughout its membership, or was it confined to certain elements?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC
utterances.text: No, no, that could not be linked to members of the SDA. This was not done as a planned exercise. People feared for their families, and it turned into an epidemic at the very end. One cannot say that this was a planned exercise.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you help me about this: What was the membership, the number of the members of your party, immediately before the war broke out in Brcko and the surrounding area, for which it was responsible?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC
utterances.text: Well, we estimate -- of course these are approximate data, but we estimate that we had approximately -- that is to say, a large number of members or sympathisers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Ramic, one politician's idea of "large" can be different from another's. When you say "large," how many do you mean? In round terms; I don't want the exact number. Are we talking 1.000, 10.000, 20.000?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC
utterances.text: Brcko, the town of Brcko was of mixed composition; that is to say, in the town itself, we had -- these are approximate figures, once again -- perhaps 10.000 members, these supporters and their families.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And certainly in my country, political parties tend to try and assess the memberships of other parties. Did you carry out such an exercise in relation to your -- if I may call it your political opponents, and try to assess how many members they'd got?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC
utterances.text: Yes, we did make assessments of that kind, and let me tell you at the outset that they were to the advantage of other parties. And after the elections, we succeeded in having a cross-section, a breakdown of these. And looking at the electoral results from all the electoral points, by finding the number of votes for a particular party and the number of members of the local population, we were able to ascertain that for the SDS and for the HDZ, between 80 to 90 per cent of the local ethnic population voted. We could say that they were their members and supporters.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What about the Social Democratic Party, which wasn't ethnically based? What sort of membership did it have? Did you assess that?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC
utterances.text: Yes. It was of a mixed composition. And related to a question you asked a moment ago, let me say that in our estimates, we established that for the votes in favour of the Social Democratic Party, these votes came predominantly from the Bosniak members; that is to say, 80 per cent of their votes came from the Bosniak electorate.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what about the Reform Coalition? From where did it draw its votes, and were you able to assess its membership?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC
utterances.text: They were of a similar composition to that of the party mentioned a moment ago, the Socialist Democratic Party. And in the same way, and that is a well-established fact, that the majority of votes came to them from voters from the Bosniak ethnic group.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Ramic, thank you, I'm finished with those for the moment again. Is this right, that at one stage, probably in the immediate run-up to the outbreak of fighting, you found yourself being followed by somebody? Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you able to identify either who they were or from what organisation those people were?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC
utterances.text: No, I wasn't able to determine that, but one could only conclude who they were.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did there come a time, in due course, when the town itself seemed to be deserted?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC
utterances.text: Only at the time when the bridges were blown up and when general chaos reigned. Then due to the population fleeing, the town was semi-deserted.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So of the -- if we can just get an idea of this: The original population in 1991 of 87.000 or so, by the time war broke out, how many of those remained?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC
utterances.text: Do you mean the overall population or only the Bosniaks?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The overall population, Mr. Ramic, please.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC
utterances.text: Well, this is a rough estimate, I haven't got exact figures, but I can say that in town at that time, about 10.000 people remained.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What proportion of that would have been Bosniak?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC
utterances.text: Well, my estimate is that there were about 3.000 to 4.000 Bosniaks of that number. Let's say 3.000, thereabouts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where had most people gone? Had they gone further into the central part of Bosnia-Herzegovina, or gone abroad, or gone to Croatia, or where did most people go?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As soon as the bridges were destroyed, let me say in a few words that, as I said, there was a general disturbance. The people were frightened. Most of them started to flee from the town. A situation of this kind lasted -- that was the situation on the 30th and on the 1st of May. So two days was sufficient time for people who wanted to leave town to do so, and that was when the population fled. Most of them went to the south, to the area where the army had not taken over power, and from there the people then started leaving, for the most part, abroad.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'd like now just to turn briefly to the incident where you were at the television station and were trying to make some sort of broadcast. Is this right: that you were -- in fact, there was a technician there, who came to you and told that you there was a telephone call for you and that you were urgently required in a particular part of Brcko? Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC
utterances.text: Yes, I remember that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You hadn't haven't, in fact, been detained or imprisoned or anything like that immediately before the television broadcast?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC
utterances.text: The aim of the garrison commander was that I should prevail upon the people of Brcko to calm down so that he enter the town after that, because he was, in fact, afraid of the citizens' reactions. It is for that reason that I was to have launched that appeal. Quite obviously he had the intention, and I saw this straightaway, as soon as I was given an escort of two armoured vehicles, because there was no need for these armoured vehicles. There had been no incidents in town anywhere at this time, so this wasn't necessary, and least of all did he need to protect me from my own citizens. Why should he protect me with two armoured vehicles?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Ramic, will you please look at the Judges when you give your answers? You are now -- you have the right to say whatever you like, but I should like you to look at the Judges when you are answering the question. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC
utterances.text: I apologise, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, it's very simple. I think we're going to have our second break now. So we shall now make a quarter of an hour break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We shall resume now and work until 6.00. Will the accused be brought in, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Greaves, the floor is yours.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Ramic, could I ask you now, please, to look at the plan of the town of Brcko? If you could just quickly indicate to us, please, so that we understand what is involved, when you refer to "free Brcko", what area of Brcko to you mean and could you indicated by pointing with the pointer on the map, please?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC
utterances.text: It's this part here, this part of Brcko [indicates], the southern/south-easterly part. Could you move the map a little bit? No, this area. You can't see that part of town.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you've indicated the area which is known as Klanac; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC
utterances.text: No, not Klanac. Klanac wasn't the free part of town. Klanac was under the attack of the aggression.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Could I now ask you to look at the larger map which has got -- could I ask you to look, please, first of all, at Brcko, and then just a little to the south of Brcko, a town called Celic. Could you indicate that on the map, please?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC
utterances.text: Here it is [indicates].

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you help us about Celic? Was that a town which had a Muslim majority before the war?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC
utterances.text: Yes. It was a 100 per cent Muslim settlement.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did Celic remain, so to speak, behind Muslim lines throughout the conflict?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC
utterances.text: It was precisely through the Celic area that the front line passed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Through the area, but did the town itself, did it remain behind and under the control of Muslim authorities?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC
utterances.text: Most of it, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm looking for it but I can't see it, but can you indicate: Is Brezovo Polje shown on this map?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC
utterances.text: I'll show you. Brezovo Polje is here [indicates].

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Just in a little small corner of what I think is Serbian, now Federal Republic of Yugoslav territory; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC
utterances.text: No. No. It is the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina but the area called the Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. What I meant is that just to the north of the river there there's a small tongue of what looks like territory of the neighbouring country, the FRY. It's just by that, is it?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was that somewhere that had a Muslim majority before the war?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC
utterances.text: Yes, there was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was the proportion of the majority there?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC
utterances.text: Well, Brezovo Polje itself has two parts to it, the Brezovo Polje village and the central region. The central region was inhabited by Bosniak Muslims, and the Brezovo Polje village inhabited by Serbs. Taken together, I would say that the ratio, that is to say not broader area, but that it was a 60/40 ratio in favour of the Muslim Bosniaks.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you now indicate the town of Razljevo, which I think is between Brcko and Bijeljlha?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC
utterances.text: Razljevo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You have to forgive me. My pronunciation is not perfect.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC
utterances.text: Here [indicates]. Here it is [indicates].

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. What was the ethnic make-up of that town before the war?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Greaves, could you please explain the reason behind these questions, because we're -- and perhaps if you could speed it up a little bit, we would be grateful.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: These are towns to which people were sent from detention facilities in Brcko, and they have been mentioned as having been so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I didn't get that during the examination-in-chief, but will you please try to focus again on the examination-in-chief, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Ramic. We can put the map away, please. If we can turn now, please, to the lists that were prepared, and in the first instance to the one marked H, please. This is the list, which you and your brother prepared, of those who had been involved in political life and were killed. Is it your evidence that all of them were killed on the first day of the conflict?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC
utterances.text: I don't know that for sure, but they were killed on the first days of the conflict. Let's say in the first ten days.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: From whom, in general, did you get the information which enabled you to say, "This person is dead. That person is dead"?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC
utterances.text: Here, of course, I cannot give that kind of information, that is to say that I saw the killings or that I saw anybody dead. All the information was gained from witnesses, eyewitnesses, people who were on the spot or who had seen the dead bodies; or the family, quite simply, up until the present day, does not know where their members are, and I can explain to you if you want to go through it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, let's just take an example, if we may, and look at the quality of your information. Look at number 14, if you would be so kind, please: Salih Hibeljic. His nickname, Djaja; would that be right?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did you hear about him, and from whom did you hear it?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC
utterances.text: Well, I heard that he had disappeared in the first days of the war. And according to my information, up until the very end of the war, I never heard anything of him, as to his being alive.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just describe him to us. He was one of your members of parliament, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC
utterances.text: Yes, he was, yes. He wasn't a member of parliament. He was on the list of members. That is to say, he was a man -- he was a butcher by profession. He lived in a part of town that we referred to as Ciganluk, or Djermanovica Sokak. He was a member in the municipal parliament. He was an elderly man, about 50 years old. As far as I remember, he had a small mustachio.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You say he wasn't a member of parliament, but I have the name "Salih Hibeljic" listed as Number 22 on the list of SDA members, so are you entirely accurate about that, Mr. Ramic?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC
utterances.text: He was on the list of those names, with those names, but he did not take part in the work of the parliament. He gave up his seat to the next one on the list.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: If Your Honour would just give me a moment, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would it surprise you to learn that he is alive and well and living in Begovaca?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC
utterances.text: It wouldn't surprise me. Why should it? He was, throughout the time, listed as missing, and as you can see, I believed until this day that he was missing and that he had been killed. But I am, of course, happy to learn that he is alive.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You see, your list is headed "Killed." Are there any other names which are in fact simply missing, and you don't actually know if they have been killed, on that list of 39, Mr. Ramic?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC
utterances.text: I'm looking through the list to check. I think that all these people were killed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I suppose that you have an element which says that these people are alive? If you have some information about that, whichever the judicial system, I believe that the Judges are entitled to have this. This is called the list of the killed. We are very happy, of course, to hear that this man is alive, and I believe that we all share that. But I hope that you have a certificate, a letter, a photograph, a document, or something to substantiate this information. Do you?

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: The point of the question is this, Your Honour, if I may explain it to you. The list is headed "Killed" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I believe this merits explanation.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: The list is headed "Killed," and the implication of the word "Killed" is -- and of his evidence is "I have information that they were killed." What he has now said is, throughout, in relation to Salih Hibeljic, he was listed as missing. There is, with respect, a considerable difference between the two, and what he has purported to say by this list is that these were all killed. The question I asked of him was, is there anybody else who was simply listed as missing, so therefore he cannot affirm that they were killed? And what I'm questioning is the reliability of this list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your previous question, which caused my concern -- I did understand the last question, but you have modified your presentation, and of course you are bringing the credibility of this witness into question, because you submitted this list of the killed persons to him and are trying to check it. And I congratulate you, that you really have the right to question his credibility if he says that all these persons were killed. But we now have -- you said, "Would you be surprised to hear that this person was alive?" Now, I allow myself to tell you that this was practically an affirmative question, not a hypothesis. It simply sounded to me that, by your question, when you said, "Would you be surprised to hear that this person is alive," I expected you to say, "Here; I am giving you the proof that that this person is alive." If not, then we have one thesis which is of the accused, and another one which comes from the witness, and that is not enough. And in the cross-examination, I'm giving you here a sample of cross-examination in common law, but of course I do it with all humility, but I believe that even if Judges do not have the right of investigation, as in some other systems, I should like, with all due respect, to ask you that when you formulate such a question, you say, "Would you be surprised to hear that this person is alive?" I would expect you to add, "Would you be surprised to learn that I," for instance, "have a certificate that he is living in such-and-such a town?" for instance.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Well, I'm not allowed to give evidence, and I'm not going to give evidence. We are in a position to call evidence as to the existence and continued life of this gentleman, not in the form of a certificate, but in the form of somebody who has met him and seen him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I understand that. I understand very well, Mr. Greaves. But I needed simply a more complete answer, and now things become much clearer for the Judges; that is, we have a witness who should have perhaps exercised much more caution in saying that such-and-such persons are killed and such-and-such are missing, perhaps. But we also have the right to ask the Defence to produce some elements to support or not, at least to give us some proof, to show us how they know that a particular person is still among the living. Thank you very much. That is what I was trying to tell you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: If I could perhaps remind Your Honour, we have already had evidence from a Prosecution witness that he's alive. If I might perhaps remind Your Honour that a few days ago, we had evidence from a Prosecution witness that this man was alive.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I congratulate you on your good memory and your vigilance, really; and that following that, we shall take note of that, Mr. Greaves. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Ramic, I would like to go through the lists with you very quickly and ask you some questions about each of the names, so that we can just see how it is that you compiled it. Confine your answers, if at all possible, to one or two words, if you can explain it. First of all, Midhat Sabanovic; from whom did you hear that he had died?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC
utterances.text: I heard that from people who -- that is to say that occurred in May 1992. I can't tell you the exact date, but let us say that it was the second half of May, and it was a person killed with three other people, together with three other people, in a house in a street -- I think the name is Djindic, and I can tell you the names of the other three individuals who were killed together with that person. And I got the information from Bosniaks who were there to take out the bodies of the people killed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And killed in their own home, or in some other place?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC
utterances.text: They were killed in a house in town, in Brcko, the same day that two of them were taken off to the Luka camp, and so, as far as I was told, were allowed to go home to fetch some things.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know who killed him?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC
utterances.text: A name was mentioned, a man by the name of Kosto or Kostic. That name was mentioned as being the name of the killer.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm not going to ask you about the second name, because we've had a lot of evidence about him. Number 3, Husein Kaknjo; from whom did you hear that he had been killed?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC
utterances.text: Husein Kaknjo was also killed in the immediate vicinity, and people saw this, near the central mosque, called the White Mosque, in the centre of Brcko, together with several other people.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you put a date on it?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC
utterances.text: I couldn't tell you dates, because we received information -- of course this information always came a little late, but it did occur in May.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you know who it was who killed him?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC
utterances.text: No, I don't know who killed him. He was killed by people who came from Bijeljina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Number 4, Smail Ribic; from whom did you hear that he had been killed?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC
utterances.text: Smail Ribic was killed in the Luka camp. I heard this from some people, detainees who were there, camp inmates, and they watched it. I'm not sure at this point whether it was the accused, the accused who tortured him and took him out. As you know, as in similar cases, shots were heard, and he never appeared again.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm not going to ask you about number 5, because we have evidence about him. Numbers 6 and 7, two people called Kartal, both brothers; would that be right?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC
utterances.text: Yes. They were brothers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: From whom did you hear that they had died?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC
utterances.text: Once again, I heard this from people who later on came -- that is to say, they were either exchanged or they escaped later on, so with a one-month delay.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And are you able to say when it was the Kartal brothers were killed?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC
utterances.text: I don't have any exact information as to that, but they were killed in the first -- perhaps two or three months.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you know who killed them?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC
utterances.text: No, I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Armin Dzaferovic?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC
utterances.text: Dzaferovic, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: From whom did you hear that that person had been killed?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC
utterances.text: I heard that from his father and his mother, because he is neighbour of mine. It was a young man. He was a member of the youth organisation of the SDA. I didn't hear any details from them, but they do believe -- his mother and father do believe that he was killed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just while we're discussing the question of the Muslim youth organisation, can you just explain a little to Their Honours the function that that organisation played within the SDA?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC
utterances.text: Well, it was the usual kind of youth organisation; that is to say, an organisation rallying young people into the SDA membership. And in that sense, of course it had its specific interests, the interests of the young population.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So the Muslim youth association would actively canvass for votes from those -- the young voters and actively canvass to get new members to join up; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC
utterances.text: That organisation was developed after the elections. It could not have had any great influence on the elections themselves, so when we're speaking about votes, they couldn't, in fact, make any contribution to the voting. But by having members amongst the younger population, yes, they could.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you receive any information as to who had killed that person?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC
utterances.text: According to the information we received, he was a member of a group of young people, and the next numbers, 9 and 10, were also these young people. It was a group of some 30 young people, in fact, who were killed, and according to our information, they were killed on the 3rd of May, and the accused took part in that killing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You weren't present at the killings of these people, were you?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC
utterances.text: I wasn't present, but does it not mean enough to you to have the words of the family or the friends? When I'm speaking about numbers 9 and 8 along with -- 9 and 10 along with number 8, I have what the parents said, and they are two brothers, and he received direct information from the accused. He came to tell him on the 4th of May that the two of them were killed in Brcko, in front of the Evrope Cafe. On the 3rd of May this happened, and he told the father of the victim on the 4th of May.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So the extent of your knowledge involving the defendant, the accused, is that he was the bringer of the news of the death of these people? That's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC
utterances.text: It happened quite by chance. He came to Bjeljina on some business, and in addition to other things, he bought some meat in a butcher's shop. I have a statement from the man he took meat from, the butcher's shop he took the meat from, and that he said this in the presence of two witnesses. So there are people who can bear those words of his out.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That wasn't quite the question that I asked. The extent of your knowledge is this, isn't it: The accused's involvement in these matters was simply bringing information to the family? That's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC
utterances.text: He gave that information not to the family, but in the butcher's shop, and he said, "Convey that to the father," of this person called Husnija Medinic, that his dead sons are lying in such and such a place.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you don't want to answer the question, we'll move on, Mr. Ramic. We've heard evidence about Irfan Topalcevic, so I won't ask you about him. Irfan Suljic, from whom did you hear that you had been killed?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC
utterances.text: Irfan Suljic is my -- a schoolmate of mine. I know him very well. And I can't, at this point, remember who brought me the information, but sources as to the death of these people were not only -- not only from one source; there were several ways in which we learnt of this. I learnt about Irfan Suljic's killing from several people.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Amongst that information, could you put a date on when it is believed he was killed?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC
utterances.text: Irfan Suljic was also killed on the 3rd, 4th, or 5th of May; that is to say, within the first three or four days.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you told who it was who killed him?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC
utterances.text: The name wasn't stated, but he was killed within a larger group of people, and not one killer was mentioned, but two or three of them were mentioned; amongst them, the accused.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Greaves, we shall have to adjourn. How much more do you think you will need for your cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: I hope about half an hour, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let us hope so, Mr. Greaves. It is quite true that you are conducting a proper investigation, finding out names, dates, places, and everything else, asking those things of the witnesses. You know that we are already in possession of some information, so perhaps you could really try to expedite matters. I'm going to ask you to do that, really. We have only two rules, as you know. You have to go along the lines of the examination-in-chief, and, of course, you have full right to bring into question the credibility of the witness. That serves justice. But we have to adjourn now and we shall then resume tomorrow morning at 10.00. Is that so, Mr. Registrar?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So we shall adjourn until 10.00 tomorrow. The meeting is adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: 6.00 p.m., to be reconvened on Thursday, the 16th day of September, 1999 at 10.00 a.m.
